label: Matt Baxter 1/3: praise that backfires (parents)
theme: why outcome praise knocks confidence, and what to praise instead
coverQuestion: Should you tell them they were the *best* player?
coverContext: Mindset coach Matt Baxter on praise that backfires

qas.q: What's wrong with "you were the best"?
qas.a: "You were the best player out there" feels lovely, but it teaches a child that their worth depends on *results*.
Praise effort, choices and *courage* instead … "I loved how you kept demanding the ball after that missed chance."
When parents step in too quickly, the child never gets to discover that they can *cope*.

quote: On the day they're not the best, the *confidence* goes with it.

label: Matt Baxter 2/3: players who've stopped improving (coaches)
theme: plateaus are normal; how to get a stalled player learning again
coverQuestion: How do you help a player who's stopped *improving*?
coverContext: Mindset coach Matt Baxter on players who've stalled

qas.q: Why do some players get stuck?
qas.a: Ability is usually still developing underneath. What turns a plateau into a problem is how the child *interprets* it.
One of the simplest tools I use is the word *YET*. "I can't beat that defender" becomes "I can't beat that defender yet."
Pick one *specific* thing to work on for the next few weeks and notice small wins.

quote: Success leaves clues, and they can be *reapplied* to the new challenge.

label: Matt Baxter 3/3: bouncing back from a mistake (parents)
theme: why some kids spiral after one mistake, and what they do instead
coverQuestion: Why do some kids *crumble* after one mistake?
coverContext: Mindset coach Matt Baxter on bouncing back mid-game

qas.a: It rarely comes down to talent. It comes down to what the child does with the *next* moment.

qas.q: What do the resilient ones know?
qas.a: Young players who bounce back have learned that a mistake is an event, not a *verdict* on them.
Notice the mistake, let it go, and put all their focus on the very next thing they can *control*.

quote: From the touchline, a parent influences more than they *realise*, mostly through their body language.
